claim: Portugal has been stopping every package received from outside the EU with no exceptions for a decade or more.
highlighted: As someone who lives in Portugal which already stops every single package you get from outside EU with no exceptions for a decade or more
paragraph:
@levelsio: As someone who lives in Portugal which already stops every single package you get from outside EU with no exceptions for a decade or more:

I can tell you how this will go
oldNote: Exceptions exist: gifts under €45 between individuals are VAT/duty-exempt, and IOSS pre-cleared shipments pass through without extra VAT collection. Also, the universal customs clearance rule for all packages only began EU-wide on 1 July 2021, not a decade or more ago.

oldSources.quote: Gifts under €45 are tax-free.
oldSources.explanation: This confirms that there is an exception for gifts between individuals under a specific value threshold.

oldSources.quote: E-commerce suppliers and marketplaces/platforms, where applicable, may use a simplified system to declare and pay VAT for distance sales of goods imported from third countries in consignments not exceeding EUR 150 (IOSS).
oldSources.explanation: Supports the claim that IOSS shipments use a pre-cleared system for VAT collection.

oldSources.quote: From 1 July 2021, the EU will introduce new VAT e-commerce rules... abolish the VAT exemption for imported goods below EUR 22 as of 1 July 2021
oldSources.explanation: Supports the claim that the rule requiring universal declaration/VAT for all packages (including low-value ones) started in July 2021.

oldSources.quote: Until 1 July 2021, postal consignments not exceeding a value of EUR 150 can be declared for free circulation without a formal customs declaration.
oldSources.explanation: Confirms that the 'no exceptions' and 'every package' requirement did not exist a decade ago.

newOutcome.note: Not every non-EU package is stopped: gifts up to €45 and low-value goods (≤€150) are often exempt from duty, and checks are risk-based, not universal. The strict VAT/customs handling stems from EU-wide rules effective July 2021, not a decade-old Portuguese policy.

sources.quote: Packages marked as gifts with a value of up to €45 are exempt from customs duties and VAT
sources.explanation: Confirms the gift exemption mentioned in the note.

sources.quote: for commercial items, VAT and customs duties apply to packages valued above €150.
sources.explanation: Confirms that low-value goods under €150 are exempt from customs duties.

sources.quote: The gift exemption threshold is up to €45 from non-EU countries.
sources.explanation: Provides additional confirmation of the gift tax-free limit.

sources.quote: Up to €150: May be exempt from customs duties
sources.explanation: Supports the claim regarding the €150 threshold for low-value goods.

sources.quote: The Portuguese Tax and Customs Authority — Autoridade Tributária e Aduaneira — enforces pre-arrival declarations, controls documentation accuracy, and applies risk-based inspections
sources.explanation: Supports the note's claim that checks are risk-based rather than universal.

sources.quote: Since 1 July 2021, the day when the new directive that amended the VAT regime came into force, all goods imported from third countries... are subjected to VAT
sources.explanation: Supports the claim that the strict VAT handling for all packages resulted from 2021 EU-wide rules, not long-standing Portuguese policy.

rationale: Both note that exceptions exist for gifts/low-value goods and that the strict EU-wide customs rule only dates to July 2021, not a decade or more.

claim: According to a 2026 Newzoo report, two-thirds of gaming time went to games more than 6 years old.
highlighted: 2/3rds of gametime went to >6 year old games!
paragraph:
- Newzoo has a 2026 report saying only ~13% of gametime went to new releases!
- 2/3rds of gametime went to >6 year old games!
oldNote: The 67% figure is PC-specific, not overall gametime: Newzoo found 67% of PC playtime went to games 6+ years old, with console platforms differing. It also comes from an earlier Newzoo report on 2024 data, not the same 2026 report cited for the ~13% new-release stat.

oldSources.quote: According to the report, last year 67% of the total hours spent playing PC games was on games that are six years old or more
oldSources.explanation: Directly supports the claim that the 67% figure is specific to PC playtime.

oldSources.quote: While the difference was less stark on consoles, it still remained, with the amount of playtime dedicated to 6+ year old games sitting at 44% on PlayStation and 49% on Xbox.
oldSources.explanation: Supports the claim that console platforms differed from the 67% PC-specific stat.

oldSources.quote: Newzoo shared highlights from its third annual games industry report, which includes data on consumer habits, such as spend and gameplay, during 2024.
oldSources.explanation: Confirms that the 67% figure comes from data for 2024, not the 2026 report mentioned in the post.

oldSources.quote: Newzoo has published its 2025 PC and Console Gaming Report... That number ticked up to 57% for 2024, according to the new report.
oldSources.explanation: Confirms that Newzoo reports are released for specific years (e.g., the 2025 report covers 2024), supporting the claim that 2024 data belongs to an earlier report than the 2026 one.

newOutcome.note: The two-thirds (67%) figure comes from Newzoo's PC-only data in an earlier report, not the 2026 global report. Newzoo's global figures for games 6+ years old were 55% (2023) and 57% (2024) of playtime, short of two-thirds.

sources.quote: The report shows that 67% of playtime goes on PC games over six years old. This is a rise on last year, but the reason for that is that last year PC wasn’t separated out, and the console playtime brought it down.
sources.explanation: Confirms that the 67% (two-thirds) figure is specifically for PC gaming, not global/combined gaming, and clarifies that including console data (global) lowers that percentage.

sources.quote: This year’s Newzoo PC/console industry report, however, puts the percentage of time that gamers spent in 2023 on games six years or older at 55%, not 61%. That number ticked up to 57% for 2024, according to the new report.
sources.explanation: Shows that for the combined PC and console market (global), the figures were 55% and 57%, which are significantly lower than the two-thirds (67%) claimed.

sources.quote: PC gamers are much more likely to be playing games that are at least six years old like Roblox, League of Legends, and Fortnite. Games like that accounted for 67 percent of PC play time
sources.explanation: Confirms that the 67% figure cited in the post belongs to PC gaming specifically.

sources.quote: About 44 percent of time on PlayStation was spent on games that came out six or more years ago. The number was 49 percent on Xbox.
sources.explanation: Provides the console-specific numbers which, when combined with PC, result in a global average lower than the claimed two-thirds.

rationale: Both notes establish the 67% figure is PC-specific (not overall/global) and from an earlier report, undermining the claim.

claim: Max Ghenis estimated MacKenzie Scott's charitable giving produced approximately 70,000 QALYs when weighting each study by causal credibility, and approximately 200,000 QALYs when taking every effect at face value.
highlighted: I built an interactive model from her own gift database: ~70,000 QALYs weighting each study by causal credibility, ~200,000 taking every effect at face value.
paragraph: Max Ghenis (incorporating his later correction into OP): I built an interactive model from her own gift database: ~70,000 QALYs weighting each study by causal credibility, ~200,000 taking every effect at face value.
oldNote: These figures are Ghenis's pre-correction numbers, not post-correction as claimed. After fixing an error that mispriced international gifts at US cost anchors, his updated estimates are ~205,000 QALYs (credibility-weighted) and ~420,000 (face value), not ~70,000/~200,000.

oldSources.quote: Update (July 13): A reader caught the model's biggest error: every health dollar was priced at US anchors, so gifts to Malaria Consortium ($10M), GiveDirectly's global program ($55M)... and similar were understated by orders of magnitude.
oldSources.explanation: Confirms that there was a major correction to the model regarding international gift pricing.

oldSources.quote: Headline: median ~70,000 → ~205,000 QALYs (credulous ~420,000); blended ~$435k → ~$148k/QALY
oldSources.explanation: Shows the specific shift from the pre-correction figures (70k) to the post-correction figures (205k and 420k).

oldSources.quote: The most important control is evidence stance: from skeptical (~205,000 QALYs — each effect weighted by how well its study identifies causation) to credulous (~420,000 — every cited effect at face value).
oldSources.explanation: Validates the current, updated estimates for the two primary reporting tiers.

newOutcome.note: These are Ghenis's ORIGINAL pre-correction figures, not post-correction. A reader flagged non-US effects used US dollar anchors, understating them. Corrected figures: ~205,000 QALYs (credibility-weighted), ~420,000 (face value) — about 2-3x higher than claimed.

sources.quote: Update (July 13): A reader caught the model's biggest error: every health dollar was priced at US anchors... Headline: median ~70,000 → ~205,000 QALYs (credulous ~420,000)
sources.explanation: This explains that the 70k and 200k figures were the original pre-correction numbers, and provides the updated figures.

sources.quote: skeptical (~205,000 QALYs — each effect weighted by how well its study identifies causation) to credulous (~420,000 — every cited effect at face value)
sources.explanation: The live site confirms the current corrected QALY estimates.

rationale: Both identify the figures as pre-correction and give the same corrected values (~205,000 / ~420,000 QALYs).

claim: On Twitter, users can see interactions between people if and only if they follow all of those people.
highlighted: You see interactions between people if and only if you follow all of them.
paragraph: Again, following is a package of six things: People can see that you follow them. They can DM you even if your DMs are closed, and perhaps you can DM them. The posts you want from them appear in your feed. The posts you don't want from them also appear in your feed. You see interactions between people if and only if you follow all of them. If they're locked it's the only way to see anything at all.
oldNote: Public replies are visible to everyone by default. X's For You feed can show posts and replies from accounts you don't follow, and anyone can view a conversation via a profile's "Tweets & replies" tab or the thread itself—no need to follow both parties.

oldSources.quote: When you reply to a tweet, that reply is public by default. Your followers can see it, and not only your followers. In most cases, anyone on Twitter can see your reply.
oldSources.explanation: Confirms that replies are public by default and visible to non-followers.

oldSources.quote: Replies can appear in several places: Under the original tweet’s thread; On your profile, in the Replies tab; In timelines or recommendations, depending on engagement and relevance
oldSources.explanation: Supports the claim that replies are visible via profile tabs, threads, and algorithmic feeds without needing to follow both parties.

oldSources.quote: I actually went into your Twitter feed anonymousely (I didn’t log in) and yes, I can see your reply to Angelsnakes in the public stream
oldSources.explanation: The source, via its comments/updates, acknowledges that public replies are visible to anyone viewing a profile or public stream, even without logging in or following the users.

rationale: no_correction_needed

claim: The paper's blog post asserts that LLMs have 'access consciousness' in functional terms, while denying the ability to evaluate potential phenomenal consciousness, but the paper itself does not take this step.
highlighted: The paper's blog post asserts that LLMs have 'access consciousness' in functional terms, while denying the ability to evaluate potential phenomenal consciousness. The paper itself does not take this step.
paragraph: The paper's blog post asserts that LLMs have 'access consciousness' in functional terms, while denying the ability to evaluate potential phenomenal consciousness. The paper itself does not take this step.
oldNote: The paper itself makes this distinction, contrary to the claim. It calls the phenomenon 'access consciousness,' a 'purely functional notion,' and explicitly states 'we take no position' on phenomenal consciousness, focusing only on functional access.

oldSources.quote: The phenomenon described above is sometimes referred to as access consciousness: out of everything the brain processes, only a subset is consciously accessible, in the sense of being poised for use in reasoning and in the direct control of action and speech . Note that access consciousness is a purely functional notion; the relationship that it has with subjective experience (sometimes called phenomenal consciousness) is widely debated. In this paper, we take no position on this issue, and instead focus on the functional role played by consciously accessible information.
oldSources.explanation: The paper explicitly defines 'access consciousness' as a functional concept and states it takes 'no position' on the relationship to phenomenal consciousness.

oldSources.quote: We stress that the introspective capabilities we observe may not have the same philosophical significance they do in humans, particularly given our uncertainty about their mechanistic basis. In particular, we do not seek to address the question of whether AI systems possess human-like self-awareness or subjective experience.
oldSources.explanation: This related paper by the same lead author also explicitly declines to address subjective experience (phenomenal consciousness).

oldSources.quote: Neuroscientists and philosophers sometimes refer to the latter type of brain activity as ‘consciously accessible,’ to distinguish it from all the other processing that goes on unconsciously. ... None of this tells us whether Claude is conscious in the way people are, or whether it feels anything at all
oldSources.explanation: The blog post makes the same functional distinction as the paper, contrary to the original post's claim that only the blog makes this distinction.

newOutcome.note: This gets it backwards. The paper itself explicitly addresses phenomenal consciousness, stating "we take no position on this issue" while calling access consciousness "a purely functional notion." It's the paper, not just the blog post, that makes this distinction.

sources.quote: Note that access consciousness is a purely functional notion; the relationship that it has with subjective experience (sometimes called phenomenal consciousness) is widely debated. In this paper, we take no position on this issue
sources.explanation: This demonstrates that the paper itself, not just a blog post, makes the distinction between access and phenomenal consciousness and explicitly takes no position on the latter.

sources.quote: "We take no position on this issue," the paper states regarding the latter, "and instead focus on the functional role played by consciously accessible information."
sources.explanation: This reporting confirms that the specific quote about taking no position on phenomenal consciousness appears directly in the research paper.

rationale: Both notes reverse the claim, showing the paper itself (not just the blog post) explicitly addresses phenomenal consciousness while limiting itself to functional access consciousness.

oldNote: There is no White House AI licensing regime. Trump's June 2026 executive order 'Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security' explicitly states nothing in it authorizes a mandatory licensing, preclearance, or permitting requirement for AI models.

rationale: no_correction_needed

claim: Research found that AI agents respond to nudges in similar ways to humans.
highlighted: AI agents respond to nudges in similar ways to humans. The paper presents this as falsifying an assumption of many agent uses, in the standard 'any suboptimal behavior means you fail' standard to which we often hold AIs.
paragraph: AI agents respond to nudges in similar ways to humans. The paper presents this as falsifying an assumption of many agent uses, in the standard 'any suboptimal behavior means you fail' standard to which we often hold AIs. For now, so long as the nudges impacting your agent are not that adversarial, it seems fine, especially since humans will have the same issue. In the long term, there are ways to control for these problems by applying more intelligence, and the price of intelligence will go down.
oldNote: The paper's core finding is the opposite: AI agents are hypersensitive to nudges, responding far more strongly than humans, even when nudges are neutral or counterproductive. This exposes "a critical behavioral gap between human and model decision-making," not similarity.

oldSources.quote: We find that LLMs not only deviate from human strategies but also often display hypersensitivity to nudges, responding more strongly than people
oldSources.explanation: Confirms that the models respond differently and more intensely than humans.

oldSources.quote: findings expose a critical behavioral gap between human and model decision-making.
oldSources.explanation: Explicitly describes a gap in behavior rather than similarity.

oldSources.quote: responding far more strongly than people (who are already sensitive to them), including in cases where the intervention is neutral or counterproductive.
oldSources.explanation: Supports the claim that models are more sensitive even to neutral or negative nudges.

oldSources.quote: despite superficial similarities to human choice distributions, such models differ in subtle but important ways. First, they show much higher susceptibility to the nudges.
oldSources.explanation: Clarifies that while there are superficial similarities, the primary finding is higher susceptibility/hypersensitivity.

newOutcome.note: The underlying research actually found AI agents are far more responsive to nudges than humans, not similarly responsive. LLM agents were described as 'substantially more susceptible' and 'behaviorally brittle' compared to human decision-making.

sources.quote: LLMs... are far more responsive to nudges than humans, such that weak cues that slightly shift human behavior have larger effects on model choices
sources.explanation: Directly supports the note's claim that agents are more responsive to nudges than humans.

sources.quote: LLM agents can be behaviorally brittle under subtle changes in choice architecture
sources.explanation: Directly supports the note's claim that models were described as 'behaviorally brittle'.

sources.quote: Recent experimental evidence suggests that LLM agents are substantially more susceptible to choice architecture intended for humans than humans themselves
sources.explanation: Directly supports the note's claim that agents are 'substantially more susceptible' than humans.

rationale: Both notes state the research found AI agents are far more (not similarly) responsive to nudges than humans.

claim: According to Exponential View's analysis, the AI economy (current sales to external end users) is growing at approximately 60% year over year.
highlighted: They conclude it is about enough to pay for infrastructure investments given 6 year depreciation of chips, and is growing at ~60% year over year, and that as tokens drop in price overall spending rises per Jevons Paradox.
paragraph: Exponential View tries to measure the state of the AI economy, defined here as current sales to external end users, not counting internal or intermediate AI payments and goods. They conclude it is about enough to pay for infrastructure investments given 6 year depreciation of chips, and is growing at ~60% year over year, and that as tokens drop in price overall spending rises per Jevons Paradox. AI is still only 0.4% of GDP, which they call a rounding error, but exponentials go fast.
oldNote: Exponential View's report states AI economy revenue growth is running near 200% year-over-year, roughly 3x faster than any historical IT platform upgrade, not ~60%. Recent quarterly growth of ~35% QoQ annualizes to about 220%.

oldSources.explanation: The jump from a $110B trailing 12-month total to a $175B run rate implies massive growth far exceeding 60%.

newOutcome.note: Exponential View's report actually cites AI revenue growing at roughly 200% year-over-year (about 3x faster than prior IT platform waves), not ~60%. The ~60% figure refers to long-run compute growth, not revenue growth.
